Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Identify the clinical presentation of lower leg stress fractures.
Describe the typical workup for a lower leg stress fracture.
Outline the typical nonsurgical and surgical treatment options for the management of a lower
leg stress fracture.
Definition
Stress fracture: A traumatic injury in which repetitive mechanical stress or overuse to the bone
causes microfractures, which may progress to complete fracture

Patient history: Focal atraumatic leg pain, most common in active individuals with a recent
increase in repetitive activities
Physical examination: Point tenderness at the fracture site; evaluation should include
identification of predisposing biomechanical causes (ie, varus or valgus alignment).

Patient Presentation
Patients with a lower leg stress fracture of the tibia or fibula often present with pain on
the involved bone in a relatively focal location rather than diffuse pain. Classically,
patients describe a recent change in the type, intensity, or duration of the repetitive
activity or exercise that preceded the onset of symptoms; however, symptoms also may
begin without any identifiable cause. Frequently, pain begins as a vague discomfort with
higher demand activities and may progress in severity to include daily activities.
Occasionally, patients describe an acute event after which their symptoms worsened.
Tibial and fibular stress fractures can occur in any patient demographic group; however,
they are more common in athletic individuals and military recruits.1 The incidence of
stress fractures is higher in females, particularly those who have the components of the
female athlete triad (low energy availability, irregular menstruation, reduced bone
density);2 however, relative energy deficiency in sport has been associated with bone
stress injuries in males.1 In patients with orthopaedic implants in the leg or who have
undergone prior joint fusions, altered stress on the bone may increase the risk for
adjacent stress fractures. For example, tibial stress fractures proximal to a
tibiotalocalcaneal hindfoot arthrodesis intramedullary nail3 or distal to a total knee
arthroplasty tibial stem have been observed.
Physical examination findings in patients with a tibial or fibular stress fractures may
include an antalgic gait or an abnormal weight-bearing pattern to offload the affected
location. Focal point tenderness directly on the bone is typical. A one-legged hop test to
acutely stress the bone may elicit pain. Evaluation of patients with a tibial or fibular
stress fracture also should include assessment of biomechanical or alignment
abnormalities, which may increase the risk for a stress injury, such as hindfoot varus or
valgus (Figure 1).

Imaging and Laboratory Studies
Plain radiographs should be obtained in patients in whom a lower leg stress fracture is
suspected. Radiographs may appear normal 2 to 3 weeks after symptom onset. Signs of
fracture healing, such as cortical thickening and callus formation, may be observed on
radiographs after several weeks. In patients who have experienced an acute event or
worsening of symptoms, the physician must be diligent in evaluating for signs of a
complete fracture, with or without displacement (Figure 2).

Figure 2
Lateral radiograph of the tibia and fibula of a patient with a chronic anterior tibial stress
fracture demonstrates an acute complete fracture. Note the cortical thickening of the
anterior tibial cortex and multiple transverse radiolucent lines indicative of a chronic
stress fracture. (Courtesy of Jeremy Y. Chan, MD, Stanford, CA.)
Tibial and fibular stress fractures usually are horizontally oriented diaphyseal fractures,
with distal third fibular stress fractures being more common than proximal fibular
fractures (Figure 3). Anterior tibial shaft stress fractures are of particular importance
because they are associated with an increased risk of delayed union or nonunion. A
dreaded black line observed at the anterior tibial cortex may be observed on a plain
lateral radiograph (Figure 4; and with advanced imaging modalities), which may prompt
urgent surgical management.

Figure 4
Lateral radiograph of a tibia and fibula demonstrates cortical thickening of the anterior
tibia and a radiolucent fracture line (dreaded black line), which indicates the need for
surgical management to decrease the risk of delayed or nonunion. (Courtesy of Jeremy Y.
Chan, MD, Stanford, CA.)
In patients with plain radiographs that appear normal despite prolonged symptoms and
patients in whom a high clinical suspicion for stress fracture exists, MRI is the preferred
advanced imaging modality because of its high sensitivity and specificity. Bone marrow
edema, which is an indication of a bone stress reaction, will be observed as a high signal
intensity on T2-weighted MRIs (Figure 5). As the stress reaction progresses to a fracture,
intracortical signal changes may be observed on T2-weighted short tau inversion
recovery MRIs (Figure 6). Linear areas of low signal intensity observed on T1-weighted
MRIs indicate a complete stress fracture (Figure 7). In addition to diagnosis, MRI findings
may have some utility in patient prognosis, with higher grade stress injuries observed on
MRI being associated with longer time to return to sports activity.4

Technetium Tc-99m bone scanning also may be used for the diagnosis of stress
fractures, showing increased uptake at the location of interest. Changes on bone scans
have been observed very soon after the onset of symptoms; however, bone scanning is a
less specific imaging modality than MRI.
Management
Nonsurgical management: activity restrictions with protected weight bearing
Surgical management: intramedullary nailing or tension plating

Management

9/13

Stress fractures of the tibia and fibula typically respond well to nonsurgical management
aimed at decreasing the level of stress on the lower leg. Changing a patient’s exercise
routine to a cross-training regimen rather than continued repetition of the same activity
may be effective. It also may allow the patient to maintain a high level of activity while
improving symptoms. Other patients may require a substantial decrease or complete
elimination of impact via protected weight-bearing in a controlled ankle motion boot or
cast. After a patient’s symptoms have improved and clinical (and radiographic, if
applicable) healing has occurred, stress should be gradually reintroduced to decrease
the risk of recurrence.
Stress fracture management should include an investigation of the contributing factors
that may have precipitated the fracture, such as training errors, malalignment, or
inappropriate equipment. In patients in whom metabolic abnormalities, such as vitamin
D deficiency or osteopenia, are suspected, evaluation of serum vitamin D levels or bone
density via dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry should be considered.2 More detailed
laboratory investigation of nutritional or endocrine abnormalities may warrant a formal
evaluation with a nutritionist or an endocrinologist to aid in targeted treatment.
Treatment also should address any alignment issues that may contribute to a stress
fracture (especially in patients in whom multiple stress fractures appear in a similar
location at separate time intervals). For example, a cavovarus foot (especially a rigid
cavovarus foot) may create increased load on the medial tibia, resulting in repetitive
medial malleolus stress fractures. A severe pes planovalgus foot may create repetitive
subfibular stress from abutment, resulting in a fibular stress fracture (Figure 1). In
situations such as these, an orthotic or brace may improve load distribution in the distal
extremity, eliminating repetitive injury to the tibia or fibula.
Surgical treatment with or without the use of concomitant biologic enhancements may
be necessary in select patients with a lower leg stress fracture.5 In patients with a tibial
shaft stress fracture involving the anterior cortex (ie, the dreaded black line), load
sharing with an intramedullary tibial nail has been used to decrease the risk of delayed
or nonunion6 (Figure 8, A and B). Alternatively, anterior tension band plating results in
high rates of union in patients with an anterior tibial stress fracture but with higher rates
of symptomatic implants7 (Figure 8, C).

Figure 8
AP radiographs of the lower leg of a patient with an anterior tibial stress fracture. The
fracture (A) was managed via tibial intramedullary nailing (B) to aid in load sharing.
Despite intramedullary nailing, the patient had a persistent symptomatic nonunion,
which resolved via anterior tension band plating (C). (Courtesy of Jeremy Y. Chan, MD,
Stanford, CA.)
In patients with a concomitant deformity, correction of a substantially malaligned foot
(ie, cavovarus or severe pes planovalgus) may indirectly assist in eliminating repetitive
load and subsequent stress injury to the tibia and fibula.
Pearls and Pitfalls
Tibial and fibular stress fractures typically result from a change in the type or duration of
activity placed on the leg.
Symptoms include focal point tenderness to palpation and activity-related pain.
Plain radiographs may appear normal for many weeks after symptoms begin.
MRI may be helpful because of its increased sensitivity in the early symptomatic period.
Nonsurgical management aimed at decreasing stress and gradually reintroducing activities is
the most common treatment option. In certain patient populations, treatment plans should
include a metabolic workup and referral to a nutritional or endocrine specialist.
Patients with an anterior tibial stress fractures in whom a fracture line is observed on
radiographs may require surgical treatment via intramedullary nail stabilization or anterior
tension band plating.
